assessment:
In this study, Piersma and colleagues address a fundamental question in natural killer (NK) cell biology: whether a single inhibitory Ly49 receptor is sufficient to license NK cells and mediate missing-self recognition. The authors generated a complete Ly49 knockout (Ly49KO) mouse using CRISPR/Cas9 to delete all Ly49 family members, then rescued function by expressing Ly49A alone from the Ncr1 locus. This elegant genetic approach overcomes limitations of previous studies where multiple Ly49 receptors with overlapping specificities confounded interpretation of individual receptor contributions.

The experimental design is rigorous and the key findings are well-supported by multiple complementary assays. The authors demonstrate that Ly49KO mice completely lack NK cell licensing, showing 73% reduction in IFNγ production upon receptor stimulation and complete inability to reject MHC-I-deficient targets in vivo. Importantly, expression of Ly49A alone fully restored both licensing (measured by IFNγ production and degranulation) and missing-self rejection to wildtype levels. The rescue of KLRG1 expression by Ly49A expressed from a different chromosome (Ncr1 on chromosome 7 versus the native Klra locus on chromosome 6) provides compelling evidence that Ly49 receptors functionally regulate KLRG1 rather than through cis-regulatory elements. The study also reveals that H-2Kb is more critical than H-2Db for missing-self recognition in the C57BL/6 background, with differential rejection efficiency depending on specific MHC-I alleles.

The evidence supporting the main conclusions is convincing, with appropriate controls throughout. The PMA/ionomycin stimulation controls confirm that defects in Ly49KO cells reflect impaired receptor-mediated activation rather than general functional impairment. The use of NKG2A-negative cells in licensing assays appropriately controls for potential NKG2A-mediated licensing. The genetic characterization of the Ly49KO mouse is thorough, including sequencing confirmation of gene disruptions and flow cytometry validation of protein loss. Minor limitations include the modest reduction in NKG2A, CD94, and NKG2D expression in Ly49KO mice, though these changes are small and the rescue experiments with Ly49A alone demonstrate sufficiency. The authors appropriately acknowledge that their findings apply to steady-state conditions and that other receptors like NKG2A may contribute under inflammatory conditions.

This work makes an important contribution to NK cell biology by definitively demonstrating that a single inhibitory Ly49 receptor is both necessary and sufficient for NK cell licensing and missing-self recognition. The findings have implications for understanding how NK cells acquire functional competence and recognize target cells, with potential relevance for therapeutic manipulation of NK cell responses in cancer and viral infections. The genetic approach establishes a valuable model system for studying individual Ly49 receptor functions without confounding effects from other family members.
